```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.4)
library(mssrscopR)
show <- function(m, main) {
  graphics::image(t(m[nrow(m):1, ]), col = grDevices::gray.colors(128, 0, 1),
                  axes = FALSE, main = main, cex.main = 0.9, asp = nrow(m) / ncol(m))
}
```

Temporal MSSR (t-MSSR) computes the single-frame MSSR map of every frame of a
sequence and then reduces the stack of maps pixel by pixel with one temporal
function (Torres-Garcia et al. 2022, Fig. 7a and Supplementary Note 5.2).
`mssr_temporal()` does this with the definitions of Supplementary Table S2.
Everything here is synthetic and generated in this document.

## A synthetic sequence

Three emitters blink independently: two close to each other and one apart.
Each frame adds Poisson noise to the blurred emitters on a faint background.

```{r data}
set.seed(7)
size <- 20
g <- expand.grid(r = seq_len(size), c = seq_len(size))
spot <- function(r0, c0) exp(-((g$r - r0)^2 + (g$c - c0)^2) / (2 * (3 / 2.3548)^2))
emitters <- cbind(spot(10, 7), spot(10, 10), spot(5, 15))
frames <- array(0, c(size, size, 60))
for (t in seq_len(60)) {
  on <- stats::runif(3) < 0.4
  frames[, , t] <- stats::rpois(size^2, 25 * (emitters %*% on) + 2)
}
dim(frames)
```

`mssr_stack()` stores the per-frame maps, so the statistics below need MSSR
only once per frame. Every per-frame setting means what it means in `mssr()`.

```{r stack}
s <- mssr_stack(frames, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
s
m <- mssr_temporal(s, "mean")
v <- mssr_temporal(s, "var")
k2 <- mssr_temporal(s, "sofi2")
v
```

```{r maps, fig.height = 2.6}
op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
show(apply(frames, c(1, 2), mean), "mean of raw frames")
show(as.matrix(m), "mean of maps")
show(as.matrix(v), "variance of maps")
show(as.matrix(k2), "SOFI2 of maps (signed)")
graphics::par(op)
```

The panels show what each statistic does to these particular frames; they do
not show that any statistic resolves the emitters better.

## Definitions

Per pixel, `x_1, ..., x_M` are the maps' values, `m` their mean and
`d_t = x_t - m`.

| `statistic` | Value | Minimum frames |
|---|---|---|
| `"mean"` | `m` | 1 |
| `"var"` | `(1/M) sum(d_t^2)`, the population variance | 2 |
| `"tpm"` | `(sum(x_t))^2 = M^2 * m^2` | 1 |
| `"cv"` | `var / m`, the supplement's "CV" (0 where `m = 0`) | 2 |
| `"sofi2"` | mean of `d_t d_{t+1}` | 2 |
| `"sofi3"` | mean of `d_t d_{t+1} d_{t+2}` | 3 |
| `"sofi4"` | fourth-order lagged cumulant | 4 |

TPM shows nothing the mean does not, for non-negative maps:

```{r tpm}
all.equal(mssr_temporal(s, "tpm")$values, 60^2 * m$values^2)
```

The SOFI statistics use signed deviations at consecutive lags, so noise that is
independent between frames does not enter their expectation. Orders 3 and 4
change sign with the emitters' duty cycle; `sign = "absolute"` returns the
absolute value for display.

```{r sofi4}
k4 <- mssr_temporal(s, "sofi4", sign = "absolute")
range(k4$values)
```

`"cv"` is literally `Var / Mean`, an index of dispersion rather than the
standard deviation divided by the mean, and it takes the sign of the mean.

## Reading the outputs

The outputs are temporal statistics of nonlinear structure maps. They are not
quantitative intensities, and no resolution gain is implied:

- Variance, `"cv"` and SOFI of per-frame MSSR maps, and higher MSSR orders, can
  show two maxima where there is a single emitter.
- When emitters are rarely on and dim, MSSR of nearly empty frames adds maxima
  to every statistic.
- `"var"`, `"cv"` and SOFI also respond to bleaching and drift (see
  `trend` below). Correct them first, and record what was done.
- With `amp > 1`, signal-free regions show a sub-pixel grid of period `amp`.
  The article recommends Fourier interpolation for temporal analysis; the
  package amplifies with the supplement's cubic kernel and mesh compensation
  instead.

`diagnostics$mesh_index` measures the grid as the range of the mean over the
`amp x amp` sub-pixel phases, relative to the mean. Where structure is present
the index would mix structure and grid, so it uses only signal-free input
pixels: by default those whose raw temporal mean is below its median, or a
`background` mask you supply.

```{r mesh}
c(m$diagnostics$mesh_region, format(m$diagnostics$mesh_index, digits = 3))
corner <- matrix(FALSE, size, size)
corner[13:20, 1:6] <- TRUE   # no emitter here
mssr_temporal(s, "mean", background = corner)$diagnostics$mesh_index
```

`diagnostics$trend` compares the raw intensity in the last tenth of the frames
with that in the first tenth. A large trend, from bleaching, drift or focus
changes, inflates `"var"`, `"cv"` and SOFI, which treat it as fluctuation; the
package reports it and corrects nothing.

```{r trend}
v$diagnostics$trend
```

## Relation to the authors' tools

The authors' Python and MATLAB "SOFI" functions use absolute deviations at zero
lag, and the Fiji plugin uses absolute deviations with lags that wrap around
the ends of the acquisition. These are other statistics, so their outputs do
not match `mssr_temporal()` by design. The authors' R, MATLAB and Fiji variance
divides by `M - 1`. `vignette("method-concordance")` lists the sources and
every difference.

## Memory and time

Statistics other than the mean and TPM need the mean before the deviations, so
they pass over the frames twice. The per-frame maps are kept for the second
pass when they fit the memory budget, and recomputed otherwise; both paths give
the same values. `mssr_estimate_resources()` reports both estimates.

```{r resources}
est <- mssr_estimate_resources(c(512, 512), fwhm = 3, amp = 2, frames = 300,
                               statistic = "var")
est[c("stack_bytes", "stored_peak_bytes", "recompute_peak_bytes")]
```
